title: ICD-10-CM Purpose and Structure

sections.learningObjectives:
- Explain the purpose of ICD-10-CM and its role in diagnosis reporting, medical necessity, reimbursement, and public health statistics.
- Describe the structure of ICD-10-CM codes, including categories, subcategories, character composition, laterality, placeholder characters, and seventh-character extensions.
- Relate the Alphabetic Index and the Tabular List and apply the look-up-then-verify workflow.
- Label the annual ICD-10-CM update cycle and its effective date.
- Recognize scope-of-practice boundaries and escalate code-assignment decisions to qualified coding staff.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

ICD-10-CM is like a giant dictionary of sicknesses. When a patient is sick, the doctor writes down what is wrong, and this book gives each problem its own special code so everyone speaks the same 'code language.'

### Question 2

Think of the letters as a label on a big worldwide book about diseases. Each word in the name tells you what the book is for: classifying diseases, and it is the tenth version, changed a little for use in clinics.

### Question 3

WHO wrote the big shared book of diseases for the whole world. The United States made a fancier, more detailed copy of that book for its own hospitals, but the world still uses the original.

### Question 4

HIPAA is a set of rules that says every doctor's office must use the same code language. For 'what is wrong with the patient,' the rule says use ICD-10-CM.

### Question 5

If the visit is a story, the 'problem' part (bronchitis) gets a diagnosis code, and the 'what the doctor did' part gets a procedure code. ICD-10-CM is for the problem.

### Question 6

Medical necessity is like needing a good reason to buy something. The diagnosis code is the 'reason' that explains why the doctor's service was needed, so the insurance company agrees to pay.

### Question 7

Doctors' offices collect millions of codes every day. When health officials add them all up, they can see which sicknesses are becoming more common, just like counting cars to see which roads are busiest.

### Question 8

Think of it as the day everyone switched to a new, bigger box of crayons. On October 1, 2015, all doctors' offices in the U.S. started using the new ICD-10-CM codes.

### Question 9

The 'CM' is like a special 'upgraded edition' label. The U.S. took the world's disease book and made a version with extra detail for doctors and hospitals here.

### Question 10

Every year, two government groups — CMS and the National Center for Health Statistics — look at the disease book and decide what new codes to add and what old ones to remove.

### Question 11

Every year, like a new edition of a calendar, the disease-code book gets refreshed on October 1 with some new codes and some removed codes.

### Question 12

Codes are like a menu that changes on a certain day each year. You must use the menu that was in effect on the exact day the patient was seen.

### Question 13

On a claim form, there are labeled boxes for different things. The diagnosis codes go in the diagnosis boxes and are connected to the services they explain.

### Question 14

ICD-10-CM is a sorting system for health problems. It puts every disease and injury into a numbered group so they can be counted and reported the same way everywhere.

### Question 15

Saying 'the left knee hurts' is more helpful than 'a knee hurts.' ICD-10-CM lets the record say left, right, or both, so the information is more complete.

### Question 16

ICD-10-CM answers 'what is wrong with the patient,' while ICD-10-PCS answers 'what procedure was done in the hospital.' They are two different code books.

### Question 17

When an insurance company asks 'why was this service needed?' the diagnosis codes are the answer on the claim. They are the proof the care was necessary.

### Question 18

Only the doctor or nurse practitioner decides the diagnosis. Everyone else's job is to help make sure that diagnosis is recorded and coded correctly.

### Question 19

Coding is like being a translator; you need training to do it right. If you are not trained, the safe move is to hand the job to someone who is, rather than guess.

### Question 20

An ICD-10-CM code is like a word that can be short or long, but it always has between three and seven letters/numbers.

### Question 21

Every code starts with a letter, like the first letter of a name. That letter tells you which big group of diseases the code belongs to.

### Question 22

After the first letter, the next two spots are always numbers, like a street address that starts with a letter then has house numbers.

### Question 23

The first three characters follow a fixed recipe (letter, number, number), but the later characters are flexible — they can be letters or numbers to add more detail.

### Question 24

The decimal point is like a divider in a phone number: the first three characters stay on the left, and any extra detail goes on the right.

### Question 25

When you write the code on a form for the insurance company, you leave out the little dot — just like dropping the dash in a phone number when you type it.

### Question 26

The first three characters are like the file folder name — a broad label for the type of problem. Extra characters are like subfolders with more detail.

### Question 27

After the broad folder name, the extra characters add details like 'which part of the body' or 'how bad,' making the code more precise.

### Question 28

For injuries, the seventh character is like a chapter marker telling whether this is the first visit, a follow-up visit, or a later problem caused by the injury.

### Question 29

A = the first time you see the doctor for the injury. D = a follow-up visit while it heals. S = a lasting problem left over after the injury healed.

### Question 30

Sometimes a code needs a blank space filled so it lines up correctly, like using a placeholder tile in a word game. The 'X' is that tile.

### Question 31

The code itself has a special spot that says 'right' or 'left.' The coder picks the code with the correct side built in.

### Question 32

The first letter is like the color of a folder: it groups together related kinds of health problems so they are easy to find.

### Question 33

The letter at the front is just a label for the group the code lives in. In I10, the 'I' marks the group of blood-pressure problems.

### Question 34

Coding is like zooming in on a map: use the most detailed view you can, as long as the doctor's notes support it.

### Question 35

Think of it as going from 'a dog' to 'a brown dog' to 'a brown dog with a blue collar.' More words (characters) means a more exact description.

### Question 36

Imagine a shelf of seven slots where a label must end in the last slot. If the label is too short, you use an 'X' to fill the empty slots so it reaches the end correctly.

### Question 37

The 'U' drawer is a special, set-aside drawer for brand-new or unusual health situations that don't fit the normal drawers yet.

### Question 38

It is like zooming in: start with the whole country (category), then the state (subcategory), then the exact city (full code).

### Question 39

A code with a dash is like a sentence cut off mid-word. You have to add the rest before you can use it.

### Question 40

A complete code is like a finished sentence: E11.9 is complete, but E11 or E1 are cut short and need more.

### Question 41

For 'which side,' the code uses a number: 1 for right, 2 for left, 3 for both, and 9 when the side is not stated.

### Question 42

The first visit is 'A' (arrival). Later check-ups while it heals are 'D' (during healing). A leftover problem after healing is 'S' (sequel).

### Question 43

ICD-10-CM codes mix letters and numbers, like a license plate, so they can hold more information than numbers alone.

### Question 44

The first three characters 'J44' are the folder label, and the '.9' is the extra detail that says 'unspecified.'

### Question 45

A sequela is like a scar left behind after a cut heals. The 'S' marker says this problem is the leftover result of an old injury.

### Question 46

More characters means a more exact description, like 'a small red ball' instead of just 'a ball.' It does not mean the problem is worse.

### Question 47

If both knees are affected, the code uses a special 'both sides' marker rather than picking just right or left.

### Question 48

The 'X' is only ever a filler in the middle or end of a code, never the first letter, because the first letter names the disease group.

### Question 49

A combination code is like a two-in-one deal: one code that already includes both the main problem and its related complication.

### Question 50

The '9' at the end is a flag that says 'we don't know the extra detail yet,' not that the code is broken.

### Question 51

The code book has two halves: a big alphabetical index to look things up, and a numbered list with the full codes and rules.

### Question 52

The Alphabetic Index works like a dictionary: find the word for the condition in ABC order to learn its code.

### Question 53

The Tabular List is ordered like numbers on a ruler — the codes go in order so you can find each one's exact spot and its rules.

### Question 54

The Index is like a map that tells you which road to take, but the Tabular List is the road itself with all the signs and rules. You must drive the road, not just read the map.

### Question 55

The main term is the bold, important word you look up first, like finding the main word in a dictionary entry.

### Question 56

Under a big word like 'bronchitis,' smaller indented words like 'acute' or 'chronic' help you pick the exact type.

### Question 57

'See' is a sign that says 'turn here instead' — you must go to the other word to find the code.

### Question 58

'See also' is like a friendly suggestion: 'you might also want to check this related spot,' but you do not have to.

### Question 59

'See condition' is a sign saying 'look up the real illness name instead' because this word is just a label.

### Question 60

When a long list runs off the page, the next page shows indented 'carryover' words so you know they still belong to the same big word above.

### Question 61

The Table of Neoplasms is a special chart that helps find the right code for a tumor by where it is and whether it is harmful or not.

### Question 62

This table is like a special list for 'what happens when a medicine or chemical harms someone,' whether by accident or on purpose.

### Question 63

The Index to External Causes answers 'how did it happen?' — the story behind the injury, like a fall or a crash.

### Question 64

Some sicknesses are nicknamed after a doctor, like a school named after a person. The index lists them under both the nickname and the real medical name.

### Question 65

You look up the main word 'hypertension' first, then find the smaller word 'essential' tucked under it.

### Question 66

First find the word in the dictionary (the Index), then check the rule book (the Tabular List) to confirm the exact code.

### Question 67

The Tabular List has 'Includes' and 'Excludes' signposts that say what belongs in a code group and what does not, like a club's membership rules.

### Question 68

The Index gives you the starting code, but you must finish the job in the Tabular List, where the side and visit-type details live.

### Question 69

Words in parentheses are like extra adjectives — 'a (big) red ball' — the word in parentheses does not change which ball it is.

### Question 70

If the doctor's notes only say 'pneumonia' without details, the coder uses the general 'unspecified' code — like using 'dog' when the notes don't say what breed.

### Question 71

Until the doctor knows for sure what is wrong, the coder writes down the symptoms — like saying 'sore throat and fever' instead of guessing a specific illness.

### Question 72

The coder is like a mirror: they must reflect exactly what the doctor wrote, not add extra details the doctor never said.

### Question 73

The default code is the 'plain vanilla' code listed right next to the main word, used when the doctor's note does not add extra details.

### Question 74

The biggest section of the Index is the 'Index to Diseases and Injuries' — the main dictionary for looking up what is wrong.

### Question 75

A combination code is a 'two-in-one' label. When it exists, you use that one label instead of two separate labels.

### Question 76

The Index is the signpost that says 'go here,' and the Tabular List is the destination where you find the full, final code.

### Question 77

First find the big word 'bronchitis,' then look under it for the smaller word 'acute' to get the exact code.

### Question 78

At the start of each chapter, the book gives directions like a rule card at the start of a game, explaining what counts and what does not.

### Question 79

'See also' is a gentle nudge to check a related spot — you add it only if the doctor's notes actually support it.

### Question 80

The Index is the map, not the destination. You still need the Tabular List to arrive at the complete, correct code.

### Question 81

Every single year, the disease-code book gets a refresh, like a yearly update to a phone's app, adding new codes and retiring old ones.

### Question 82

Using last year's app version can make things break. Using last year's codes can make the claim come back rejected.

### Question 83

New codes go live on a specific day, October 1, like a law that starts on a set date. Before that day, you keep using the old ones.

### Question 84

If you find the office is using an old, torn map, the safe move is to tell the person in charge so everyone gets a new map before driving.

### Question 85

The doctor is the one who figures out the diagnosis, and the coding team turns the doctor's words into the right code — like a translator, not the author.
